I think in this situation, yes, YTA (you're the asshole) for ignoring the homeless person who wanted money. It's understandable that working in a big city with a large homeless population means you get approached a lot, and after a while, it can be draining or make you feel cautious—especially if you've had personal or witnessed incidents that were aggressive, or if repeated requests for money feel persistent. I get that you recognize many people you see on the street and have previously made an effort to be receptive and help when possible.

But in this case, the homeless man was simply asking for food just like everyone else he approached. When you waved him off and pulled your boyfriend closer, you signaled that you were unwilling to even acknowledge his humanity in that moment. I know feeling uncomfortable is valid, but completely shutting someone down—especially when past interactions seem to be coloring your present behavior—can come across as harsh and dehumanizing. The man cursing at you wasn’t acceptable, but it seems like the situation escalated because of the cold shoulder given, leading to a verbal back-and-forth and you losing your temper.

In big cities, compassion fatigue is real, but at the end of the day, we’re all people trying to get by. I think taking a second to just say “Sorry, I can’t help today” would have been kinder and could have avoided the confrontation. Being cautious is fine, but ignoring someone outright or acting as if they’re not there only further alienates people who are already marginalized. So yes, in this scenario, I think you were in the wrong for how you responded.

Honestly, I don’t think I’m the a-hole for ignoring a homeless person who was asking me for money. I work in a big city where there’s a large homeless population, and I’m approached *constantly* for money or food, often by the same people because I recognize them. When I first moved here, I genuinely tried to be receptive and compassionate—I’d chat, offer a snack, or spare some change.

But after a while, both personal and things I’ve witnessed made me realize you never really know who might react aggressively. I started to feel way less safe. On top of that, even polite conversations more often than not turned into persistent requests that made it hard to walk away cleanly.

Just recently, there was a homeless man approaching people for food on my route. When he turned to me, I honestly just wasn’t comfortable, so I quickly waved him off and held onto my boyfriend a bit tighter. That’s when he started cursing at me—and then we found ourselves in a back-and-forth argument. I definitely lost my temper.

I wish I could always respond kindly, but after so many experiences, I don’t think it’s fair to judge me for protecting myself and setting boundaries. Until our society comes up with real solutions for the homeless, people living and working in cities shouldn’t be expected to put themselves in uncomfortable—even risky—situations all the time. So yeah, *not* the a-hole here.

Honestly, after reading everything, I think YTA in this situation. Here’s why:

At the train station, you and your boyfriend were just waiting for your train when a homeless man started approaching people asking for food. When he came up to you, you felt uncomfortable and waved him off, even pulling your boyfriend closer. That already sent a signal of rejection, which probably hurt the guy. Then he cursed at you, and things escalated into a heated verbal exchange between the three of you. You said you ended up losing your temper. Afterwards, your boyfriend told you your actions were wrong because you made the man feel less than human.

I get that it’s uncomfortable to be approached by a stranger, especially if you’re not sure what their intentions are. But just ignoring him and then responding angrily when he lashed out didn’t help the situation. Everyone deserves to be treated with some basic dignity, no matter their circumstances. Your boyfriend was right—it probably did make the man feel dehumanized, especially if all he was asking for was food. So yeah, in my opinion, ignoring a homeless person who was just trying to ask for help, then reacting harshly, does make you TA here. Next time, maybe try just saying “Sorry, I can’t help” politely—you never know what someone else is going through.

Here’s my take on this situation:

So, the other day at a train station, I was waiting for my train with my boyfriend. There was a homeless man going around asking people for food. When he approached me, I felt pretty uncomfortable, so I just waved him off and pulled my boyfriend a little closer. I guess he didn’t like that, because he started cursing at me, and things escalated into a verbal argument between the three of us. I ended up losing my temper. Afterwards, my boyfriend said I was out of line and that my reaction made the man feel less than human.

Honestly, I don’t think I’m the one at fault here. Nobody should be obligated to engage with strangers if they feel unsafe or uncomfortable, regardless of the person’s situation. It’s sad that the homeless man is struggling, but that doesn’t mean I should be forced to interact if I don’t want to. It’s not fair to accuse someone of being heartless for just wanting to protect their own boundaries and safety. So, no, I don’t think I was wrong for ignoring him. I just did what felt right for me in the moment.

Honestly, after reading all the details, I do think YTA in this situation. In my opinion, you could’ve just said a polite “Sorry, I don’t have anything to give,” and not made it feel so dismissive or confrontational right away. So, based on the facts, I do think YTA for how you handled the encounter.

But in this specific moment, the man approaching you and asking for food doesn't sound threatening on its face—he was just trying to get help, like he did with others before you.

Afterwards, your boyfriend made a good point: your actions did make the man feel less than human.

I know it's hard when past experiences make you cautious, but that doesn't excuse treating someone like they're invisible or dangerous just because they're homeless. At the end of the day, yes, you were wrong to ignore him like that. Sometimes humanity is uncomfortable, but it's important.
